1141.quote_or_event: “Slander me, slander me - go ahead, people, and slander me. ... The slanderer wishes me long life.”
1141.explanation: Bhagat Kabir welcomes the talk people spread about him, saying that the slanderer, without meaning to, actually wants him to live.
1141.tie_back: The Kural's lover says the town's gossip keeps his ebbing life from slipping away, though the gossips do not know it; Kabir likewise finds that the slander aimed at him only gives him life.
1141.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 339, Raag Gauree, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1141._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa), two lines of one shabad joined by an ellipsis; reasonable fit on hostile talk that unwittingly sustains the one talked about, but Kabir means slander that purifies the devotee, not gossip about a love affair.

1142.quote_or_event: “One who slanders me is my friend; the slanderer is in my thoughts.”
1142.explanation: Kabir turns the slanderer into a friend, because the talk against him serves his spiritual good.
1142.tie_back: In the Kural the town, not knowing how hard the girl is to win, hands the lover a rumour and so does him a favour; Kabir likewise counts the one who spreads talk about him a friend.
1142.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 339, Raag Gauree, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1142._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); reasonable fit on the unwitting favour done by gossips, though the Kural's rumour helps a courtship while Kabir's slander helps the soul shed its faults.

1143.quote_or_event: “If I am slandered, I go to heaven; the wealth of the Naam, the Name of the Lord, abides within my mind.”
1143.explanation: Kabir says that being slandered is pure gain for him, since it brings him nearer to the Lord and settles the Name in his mind.
1143.tie_back: The Kural's lover asks whether the rumour the whole town knows is not a gain to him, making him feel he has the union he has not yet won; Kabir likewise counts the town's talk as a gain that brings him to the Beloved.
1143.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 339, Raag Gauree, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1143._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); reasonable fit on talk counted as gain, but the gain is spiritual (the Name and heaven), not a foretaste of a lover's union.

1144.quote_or_event: “His love increases day by day, and when it is weighed, it does not decrease.”
1144.explanation: Guru Arjan describes the devotee whose love for the Lord keeps growing and never shrinks when tested.
1144.tie_back: The Kural's love grows and blooms on the town's gossip and would shrink without it; Gurbani speaks of a love that grows day by day and never shrinks.
1144.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1074, Raag Maaroo, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1144._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); next-best match: it shares the image of growing love, but Gurbani does not make love depend on rumour, and the love is spiritual, for God.

1145.quote_or_event: “Do not drink the false wine at all, if it is in your power. O Nanak, the True Guru comes and meets the mortal; by His Grace, one obtains the True Wine.”
1145.explanation: Guru Amar Das forbids ordinary intoxicating drink and offers instead the 'True Wine' of the Name, received through the Guru by grace.
1145.tie_back: The Kural compares love made public to toddy that grows sweeter each time the drinker is merry; Gurbani takes the same image of intoxication but redirects it to the true, sober intoxication of the Name.
1145.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 554, Raag Bihaagraa (Bihaagre ki Vaar, salok), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1145._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); partial fit on the intoxication image, with an honest conflict: Sikh teaching rejects alcohol outright, so it uses the Kural's toddy simile only to replace it with the 'wine' of the Name.

1146.quote_or_event: “The news spread throughout the world, and the beings of the three worlds came.”
1146.explanation: Guru Ram Das describes how word of the Guru's coming spread far and wide, drawing countless people.
1146.tie_back: The Kural's heroine saw her beloved only once, yet the news spread everywhere like word of an eclipse; Gurbani likewise pictures one event whose news travels through the whole world.
1146.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1116, Raag Tukhaari, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1146._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); next-best match only: it shares the image of news spreading far from a single event, but the news is of the Guru's visit, not a lovers' rumour, and there is no eclipse image.

1147.quote_or_event: “Make your mind the farmer, good deeds the farm, modesty the water, and your body the field.”
1147.explanation: Guru Nanak builds a farming metaphor in which the mind, deeds, modesty and body each play a part in raising the crop of the Name.
1147.tie_back: The Kural pictures love-sickness as a crop with gossip for manure and the mother's harsh words for water; Guru Nanak uses the same farmer's allegory, naming the water and the field that make the spiritual crop grow.
1147.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 595, Raag Sorath, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1147._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); the allegorical structure (crop, water, field) closely matches, but what grows is the Name rather than love-sickness, and the inputs are virtues rather than gossip and scolding.

1148.quote_or_event: “as fire is not satisfied by fuel.”
1148.explanation: In the Sukhmani, Guru Arjan compares the slanderer's restless envy to a fire that is never satisfied however much fuel is fed to it.
1148.tie_back: The Kural says hoping to quench love with gossip is like pouring ghee on a fire; Gurbani uses the same image of fire that only grows when fed, here for the talk of the slanderer.
1148.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 280, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1148._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa), quoted as a half-line; the fire-and-fuel image is close to the Kural's fire-and-ghee, but Gurbani applies it to the slanderer's insatiable envy rather than to love fed by gossip.

1149.quote_or_event: “You are my honor; You are my decoration.”
1149.explanation: Guru Arjan places all his honour (pat) and adornment in the Lord alone, so that what the world says can neither give nor take it away.
1149.tie_back: The Kural's heroine, already shamed by her lover's leaving, asks why she should still fear the town's gossip; Gurbani answers that one whose honour rests in the Beloved need not fear what people say.
1149.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 181, Raag Gauree, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1149._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); next-best match only: it shares the idea of honour that gossip cannot touch, but has nothing of the broken promise ('do not fear') or the abandoned heroine, and the Beloved is God, who in Sikh teaching never abandons.

1150.quote_or_event: “Whatever I ask for, I receive; I have total faith in my Master.”
1150.explanation: Guru Arjan expresses complete confidence that the Master will grant whatever His devotee asks.
1150.tie_back: The Kural's companion is sure that, with the town raising the very rumour they wanted, the lover will gladly grant what they ask; Gurbani shows the same confident trust that the Beloved will give what is asked.
1150.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 619, Raag Sorath, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1150._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); next-best match: it shares the confident expectation that the beloved will grant the request, but lacks the Kural's scheming about rumour and elopement, and the trust is in God.
